Text-to-SQL Research — Architecture, Results, and SOTA Comparison

0. Spider 2.0-Snow Benchmark

Spider 2.0-Snow is the Snowflake partition of the Spider 2.0 benchmark — the hardest publicly available Text-to-SQL evaluation suite. It contains 547 natural-language questions over 152 enterprise Snowflake databases, spanning finance, healthcare, geospatial, public transit, climate, blockchain, and more. The gold SQL references 1,415+ distinct tables across those databases. Our local schema index covers 285 tables, 8,572 columns, and 194 VARIANT sub-fields. 107 of the 547 instances also require reading external knowledge documents (PDFs, spreadsheets) to resolve domain terms before writing any SQL.

What makes this benchmark hard:

  • Multi-source joins — trips, weather, and geo-boundary tables must be linked by coordinate point-in-polygon tests, not simple key joins.
  • Temporal complexity — moving averages with lag differences, time-lagged metrics (1 h / 1 d / 7 d / 14 d ago), cross-join to fill zero-count hours.
  • Heterogeneous date encodings — epoch microseconds, epoch milliseconds, integer YYYYMMDD, and native DATE columns coexist across tables.
  • VARIANT / semi-structured data — nested JSON fields and LATERAL FLATTEN required for blockchain and GA360 tables.
  • Graph traversal — multi-hop transaction path queries over blockchain data with chronological ordering constraints.

Representative example questions

sf_bq136 · CRYPTO · Graph traversal + chronological ordering + string formatting

Find all exactly 2-hop transaction paths on the Zilliqa blockchain between a given source and destination address, considering both regular transactions and contract transitions. Exclude intermediate addresses with more than 50 outgoing transactions (exchange/high-activity filter). Ensure transactions follow chronological order. Display results as '<source> --(tx ABCDE..)--> <intermediate> --(tx FGHIJ..)--> <destination>' with transaction IDs truncated to the first 5 characters. Include only confirmed on-chain transactions.

sf_bq050 · NEW_YORK_CITIBIKE_1 · Multi-source join (trips + weather + geo boundaries)

Analyze NYC Citi Bike trips in 2014, linking trip data with Central Park weather station records to understand how temperature, wind speed, and precipitation affect ridership between neighborhoods. For each start-neighborhood × end-neighborhood pair: total trips, average trip duration (min), average temperature, wind speed, and precipitation at trip start, and the month with the most trips. Neighborhoods are resolved by mapping trip coordinates into zip-code polygons (geo_us_boundaries.zip_codes), then joining to borough/neighborhood names (cyclistic.zip_codes).

sf_bq031 · NOAA_DATA · 8-day moving averages + lag-1 through lag-8 differences

Daily weather data for Rochester (Jan 1 – Mar 31, 2019): temperature (°C), precipitation (cm), and wind speed (m/s). For each variable compute the 8-day moving average (current day + 7 prior). Then compute the difference between today's moving average and the moving averages from each of the previous 1 through 8 days (lag1–lag8). Round all values to 1 decimal place. Output ordered by date starting from Jan 9, 2019 (first day with a full 8-day window).

sf_bq293 · NEW_YORK_GEO · Geospatial join + cross-join for zero hours + 4 time-lag metrics + moving averages

NYC yellow taxi trips on January 1, 2015: join pickup coordinates to zip-code polygons, then cross-join distinct zip codes × distinct hours to produce a complete hour-by-hour grid (including zero-trip hours). For each zip code + hour: total trips plus time-lagged counts at 1 h, 1 d (24 h), 7 d (168 h), and 14 d (336 h) ago; 14-day and 21-day moving averages and standard deviations of trip counts (excluding current hour). Valid coordinates only. Return top 5 zip-code/hour groups by trip count.

PART 1 — GOLD-ASSISTED SOLUTION

The gold-fed system uses the reference answer as a stopping signal during self-refinement. This is the research ceiling — not deployable accuracy. It is the cleanest setting for isolating component value because the oracle removes selection ambiguity.

1. Architecture

Five layers, each addressing a concrete failure class in enterprise Text-to-SQL.

Layer 1 — Hybrid retrieval index

What: BM25 + text-embedding-3-large with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (k = 60) over a purpose-built entity-oriented index stored in ChromaDB.

Why: Full-schema prompting fails on enterprise warehouses (3 000+ columns). Retrieving the right schema cards rather than dumping everything is the prerequisite for every other layer.

Index cards (one discrete metadata element each):

Card type What it captures
TableCard Table name, description, row count, business role
ColumnCard Column name, type, description, sample values, cardinality hint
JoinCard Explicit join relationships (FK, implicit, common-key)
SemanticCard Typed semantic facts per column/table: time columns, metric/dimension candidates, nested containers, identifier columns, filter value hints, column stats — inferred from 4 sources: schema metadata (heuristics), external docs (regex scan), live DB probes, and execution traces
SampleRecord Representative row values per table (value grounding)
TraceMemory Successful past query traces (not yet wired into production path)
SnowflakeSyntax Dialect tips: LATERAL FLATTEN, VARIANT access, NULLS LAST, date casts
SemanticCard examples — how facts look in the LLM prompt

Partition collapsing: temporally-sharded sources (GA360: 366 daily tables, GA4) are collapsed at index-build time into one representative TableCard per logical table. Without this, GA360 schema linking is retrieval-noise — the 366 shards overwhelm retrieval ranking.

SchemaSlice post-processing: after retrieval, a deterministic multi-stage filter trims the retrieved set further: - Protected identifiers (join columns, time columns) resist trimming - 1-hop join-graph expansion: add tables reachable via one FK hop from any retained table - VARIANT enrichment: inject SnowflakeSyntax cards for tables with nested JSON/ARRAY columns

Retrieval recall — measured on 43 instances with gold SQL. Schema Retrieval Rate (SRR): fraction of instances where all gold-SQL-referenced tables appear in our retrieved schema slice (embedding + BM25 hybrid, no LLM calls), with date-sharded partition tables excluded from the required set (our deliberate design choice — shard tables are collapsed to a single representative schema card).

top-k SRR Notes
8 (production default) 86.0% (37/43) —
20 88.4% (38/43) +1 recovered instance vs. top-8; remaining misses are cross-schema semantic-distance gaps (e.g. geo tables in a different schema than the query's main tables), not fixed by depth alone
APEX-SQL Strict Recall Rate (reference) 88.33% N=120 pilot, same benchmark; requires two LLM pruning passes per query

Economic advantage: our embedding + BM25 hybrid retrieval achieves 86.0–88.4% SRR (top-8 to top-20) with zero LLM completion tokens in the schema-linking step — compared to APEX-SQL's 88.33% which requires two LLM pruning passes per query (~14k tokens). For production workloads where schema linking runs on every query, this is a meaningful cost advantage at comparable recall.

Layer 2 — Plan → SQL compiler (deterministic)

What: the LLM does not emit SQL directly. It emits a structured QueryPlan (YAML/JSON describing tables, columns, joins, filters, aggregations, output columns). A deterministic Python compiler transforms the plan into Snowflake SQL.

Why: the LLM's syntactic priors are wrong for Snowflake. LATERAL FLATTEN, VARIANT:field, TO_TIMESTAMP(col/1e6)::DATE, quoting rules — prompting doesn't reliably override these. A compiler that owns syntax closes the entire class of dialect-formatting errors.

Effect: the LLM owns intent; the compiler owns correctness. Semantically correct plans that would have produced syntax errors now execute.

Current compiler plan types: PlanSelect, PlanAggregate, PlanJoin, PlanFlatten, PlanCTE, PlanWindowFunction, PlanDateShard. PlanGeoJoin/PlanGeoFilter are partially implemented (geospatial is the largest remaining gap — see §5).

Layer 3 — Best-of-N with structural strategy diversification

What: generate N SQL candidates, each from a structurally different prompting strategy, then select the best by a multi-signal selector.

Strategies (cycled by index, one per candidate):

All strategies share the same two-step pipeline — the LLM produces a structured JSON plan, a deterministic compiler emits Snowflake SQL. The strategy is a single extra instruction prepended to the plan-generation system prompt, biasing where the LLM starts reasoning:

Strategy Opening instruction to LLM Targets
default (no extra hint) General queries
flatten_first Start by identifying VARIANT/ARRAY columns needing LATERAL FLATTEN Nested / semi-structured data
cte_first Break the question into sequential steps; each step becomes a CTE Multi-step aggregations, ranking, set ops
join_first Start by identifying the correct JOIN relationships; build outward from joins Multi-table joins
metric_first Start by identifying the target metric/aggregation, then trace back to sources COUNT/SUM/AVG questions
time_first Start by identifying date/time filters or time-based grouping Time-series, date-range filters
geo_first Start by identifying geospatial predicates (STWITHIN, STDWITHIN, radius…) Spatial / location queries

Rotation order for N=4: default → flatten_first → cte_first → join_first. For N=8 all seven strategies fire, then default repeats. Temperature ramps from T=0.2 (candidate 1) to T=0.3 (candidates 2+) for additional stochastic diversity on top of the structural hint.

This creates structural diversity, not stochastic re-sampling of the same prompt.

Selection (multi-signal): the selector scores candidates on: (1) execution success, (2) result non-emptiness, (3) result-set agreement across candidates (self-consistency voting), (4) fingerprint verification, (5) metamorphic check, (6) learned verifier score (when trained).

Gold-fed mode: gold result is used as an additional selection signal — the selector picks the candidate whose executed result matches gold. This is the oracle that creates the gold-fed ceiling.

Layer 4 — Self-correction repair loop

What: after a candidate executes (success or error), an LLM-driven repair loop inspects (question, SQL, execution result or error) and attempts targeted fixes.

Gold-fed signal: when --gold_dir is active, the loop injects a synthetic RESULT_MISMATCH error if the result differs from gold — driving repair even on executing-but-wrong SQL.

Error categories (8 Snowflake-specific classes): SYNTAX_ERROR, COLUMN_NOT_FOUND, TYPE_MISMATCH, RESULT_MISMATCH, EMPTY_RESULT, WRONG_AGGREGATION, WRONG_JOIN, VARIANT_ACCESS_ERROR

Each category triggers a different repair prompt with category-specific guidance (e.g. VARIANT_ACCESS_ERROR hints at :field vs ['field'] vs GET_PATH).

Budget: max_repairs attempts per candidate (typically 3–4). Repair stops on gold match (gold-fed) or when the budget is exhausted.

Layer 5 — Verification (fingerprint + metamorphic)

What: two lightweight post-execution checks applied to each Best-of-N candidate before final selection. Their score_delta feeds directly into the selector scoring formula.

Fingerprint check

Builds a structural summary of the execution result — not a simple hash. Captured fields: row_count, column_names, null_ratios per column, and numeric_stats (min/max/mean for up to 5 numeric columns). Stored alongside every candidate; feeds the verifier feature vector for any future learned verifier model. Catches structurally identical results across candidates so the selector can group them.

Metamorphic checks (up to 2 per candidate)

Check A — Shape consistency (no extra SQL execution). The system infers the expected answer shape from the NL question, then compares against the actual result:

Situation Example question signal Score delta
Grouped output expected, only 1 row returned "breakdown by region" → result has 1 row −15
Aggregate expected, 1 row confirmed "total revenue" → result has 1 row +10
Monthly time-series, 6–24 rows returned "monthly trend over the past year" → 12 rows +10
Daily time-series, ≥7 rows returned "daily sessions last week" → 7 rows +5
Small result expected, ≤5 rows returned "top 5 customers" → 5 rows +5
Aggregate expected but multiple rows returned "total orders" → 47 rows −5

Check B — Limit expansion (requires one extra execution). If the SQL contains LIMIT N, re-runs it with LIMIT N*2. If the expanded query fails, the original is likely structurally fragile — not just data-dependent. Failure docks −5 points. Example: LIMIT 10 → re-run as LIMIT 20; if the doubled query errors, penalise the candidate.

Observation: both checks fired 0% on the ablation's 25-query slice — targeted at failure modes that appear at scale or in pathological query types (GA360 time-series, geospatial aggregates, heavily nested VARIANT access).

2. Gold-fed results

2a. Headline — 100-query benchmark (Best-of-N = 8, three independent runs)

The primary gold-fed result: the full system run across 100 representative Spider 2.0-Snow instances (broader than the ablation slice — includes geospatial databases), replicated three times to estimate variance. Model: gpt-5.4-mini. Best-of-N = 8, max_repairs = 4.

Run Accuracy
benchmarkrun10 87% (87/100)
benchmarkrun11 81% (81/100)
benchmarkrun12 84% (84/100)
Mean 84% (range 81–87%)

The gold-assisted full system solves ~84% of a representative 100-query Snow set. Run-to-run variance ±3 pp is real: the ±3 pp band is not noise — it reflects a genuine 14-query flaky core that sometimes succeeds, sometimes doesn't (stochastic sampling at temperature 0.2).

Per-instance stability:

Outcome Count
Always correct (3/3 runs) 76
Flaky (1–2 of 3 runs) 14
Never correct (0/3 runs) 10

Reliable solved core: 76%. Hard unsolvable core: 10%. The honest "reliable capability" is 76%; the best-case is 87%; the mean ceiling is 84%.

Domain breakdown (majority of 3 runs):

Database Solved
GITHUB_REPOS 15/15 ✅
NOAA_DATA 12/12 ✅
PATENTS 14/15 ✅
GA360 10/12 ✅
CMS_DATA 7/7 ✅
CENSUSBUREAUACS_2 2/4 ⚠️ retrieval noise on 296-table schema
GEO_OPENSTREETMAP 3/6 ❌
NEWYORKNOAA 1/3 ❌
NEWYORKCITIBIKE_1 1/3 ❌

Geospatial (ST_* / distance predicates) is the dominant weak domain. Conventional analytics (patents, GitHub, weather, GA360, healthcare) are handled well at Best-of-N = 8.

Connection to ablation: the 30-query component ablation showed Best-of-N is the dominant component (+80 pp). This 100-query run is that recipe at its strong setting (N=8 + 4 repairs), confirming the finding scales: the same architecture that scores 90% on the easier 30-query non-geo slice scores 84% on the harder geo-inclusive 100-query set.

Key readings: - Best-of-N uses 4× tokens for +80 pp accuracy — unambiguously worth it. - Repair loop costs ~2× tokens for +16.7 pp — real but the CI floor touches 0. - Knowledge components (semantic, sample-records, verifier, verification) show no statistically reliable gain at n=30 — not proven useless (true +5–10 pp effects are invisible at n=30), but require validation at larger N before further investment.

2c. Interpreting the gold-fed number — what it means and doesn't

Gold is consumed in two separate places: 1. Selection — pick the best-of-N candidate whose result matches gold 2. Repair — keep iterating toward gold until it matches

The ablation's no_repair arm removed only the repair iterations with gold selection still on. So "+16.7 pp for repair" means the value of iterative repair given gold-assisted selection — not the value of gold itself.

Config Gold for selection? Gold-driven repair? Accuracy
Full gold-fed ✅ ✅ ~84–90%
No-repair arm (ablation) ✅ ❌ ~73%
No gold at all (deployable) ❌ ❌ ~33–60%

Going to no-gold removes the signal from both — and the bigger loss is selection (~40 pp combined), not the repair loop (~17 pp). The gold-fed ceiling is the target a good no-gold verifier would chase; it is not deployable accuracy.

PART 2 — NO-GOLD (DEPLOYABLE) SOLUTION

No gold oracle at any point during inference. Scored post-hoc by running predictions against gold after the fact, with the agent fully blind.

3. What changed: the no-gold architecture

3a. Self-consistency / MBR voting (replaces gold-assisted selection)

Candidates are clustered by an order-insensitive signature of their executed result (not SQL text). A candidate receives consensus_bonus × (independent_votes − 1), where a "vote" counts only from a distinct strategy — so running the same strategy twice cannot inflate its score. The candidate with the highest total bonus wins.

Why result-clustering, not SQL-text clustering: two queries with different SQL but identical result sets are equivalent. Result-cluster voting selects by semantic correctness, not syntactic similarity.

Why consensus works: independent strategies produce the same result only when they agree on table semantics, join path, and aggregation logic. Accidental agreement across structurally diverse strategies is rare; genuine agreement is evidence of correctness.

3b. Self-critic repair loop (replaces gold-driven RESULT_MISMATCH)

An LLM inspects (question, SQL, result preview) and, if it diagnoses a concrete error, drives a repair attempt. It never marks a successfully-executing SQL as failed — it only spends extra repair budget when it finds a specific problem.

Diagnostic quality vs repair quality: the self-critic's diagnoses are model-independent (both gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.4 produce sharp diagnoses like "returns only one month but the question asks for June and July", "scans only EVENTS_20210131 so the Jan 1–7 filter can't access those dates"). But repair quality is model-dependent — only gpt-5.4 can translate a correct diagnosis into a fixed query. This is the model × method interaction.

Error classification and repair dispatch: each error is classified into a type and routed to a targeted repair prompt:

Error type What it means Repair strategy
invalid_identifier Column or alias name does not exist Inject the exact offending identifier; instruct LLM to use only schema-confirmed names
object_not_found Table or view does not exist Inject the offending object name; enforce schema-only object references
aggregation_error Non-aggregated column absent from GROUP BY Force CTE rewrite; separate measures from dimensions
empty_result SQL executes but returns zero rows Relax filters; check date encoding format; try ILIKE for string matching
result_mismatch / self_critique Executed but result is wrong or suspect Re-read question; verify joins, filters, aggregation logic, and date range
recursive_cte Recursive CTE dialect error Prescriptive Snowflake WITH RECURSIVE template with anchor/recursive arm rules
general Type mismatch, unknown function, syntax, other Generic repair with full schema context

Robustness guard: on sf_bq269 the critic's repairs pushed all 4 candidates into sql_syntax_error (baseline: wrong-but-executing → improved: broken). Fix: revert to the last successfully-executing SQL when a repair breaks execution.

3c. Exploration front-end

Runs read-only SQL probes before generating the answer query. Two mechanisms run in sequence, both operating on the already-retrieved schema slice (typically 5–15 tables), not the full warehouse.

Mechanism 1 — deterministic date profiling (profile_date_columns)

Iterates every column in the schema slice and fires on two conditions: the column has is_time_column=True in the index, or its name matches (date|time|created|modified|timestamp|_at$|_dt$|_ts$). Action depends on the declared type:

  • Native DATE / TIMESTAMP types — records the fact immediately, zero DB queries.
  • Numeric or VARCHAR with a date-like name — runs SELECT MIN(col), MAX(col) to classify encoding from magnitude (≥10¹⁴ → epoch micros, ≥10¹¹ → millis, ≥10⁸ → seconds, 8-digit → YYYYMMDD integer).

The DB-query part is hard-capped at 8 probes. Results feed both the prompt (authoritative format facts) and a rewrite map used by the deterministic rewriter in §3d.

Mechanism 2 — LLM-generated probes (max 6)

The LLM reads the question + schema slice and writes up to 6 read-only probe SQLs. It is instructed to prioritise in this order:

  1. Date/time filter columns — MIN/MAX + raw LIMIT 5 sample to confirm encoding before any date filter is attempted.
  2. Entity / literal resolution — SELECT DISTINCT col WHERE col ILIKE '%keyword%' LIMIT 20 for values the question names (station names, ticker symbols, category codes, etc.).
  3. Categorical filter columns — SELECT col, COUNT(*) GROUP BY … ORDER BY DESC LIMIT 10 to surface top values.
  4. VARIANT / ARRAY structure — LATERAL FLATTEN … LIMIT 5 to discover nested field names before writing any :field access.

The LLM picks the 6 most relevant probes for this question — it does not probe every filter column. A question referencing 10 entities will only probe the most query-critical ones.

Overhead budget: at most 8 + 6 = 14 lightweight Snowflake round-trips per question. In practice fewer, because native timestamp types cost zero probes, the LLM typically writes 3–5, and every probe is a MIN/MAX, DISTINCT LIMIT, or FLATTEN LIMIT — no full table scans. All probe failures are silently swallowed; a failed probe contributes no evidence and does not block generation.

Results feed the prompt as grounding facts, replacing model guesses with real database evidence.

3d. Deterministic data-format enforcement

Problem: the model's priors (e.g. "date = YYYYMMDD") override soft prompt hints reliably. A query that should use TO_TIMESTAMP(col/1e6)::DATE will get CAST(col AS DATE) from prompting.

Solution: code-level rewrite rules that detect and fix: - Epoch-microsecond integer columns: col → TO_TIMESTAMP(col/1e6)::DATE - Native date columns incorrectly cast: fix to DATE 'YYYY-MM-DD' literals - VARIANT access: normalize :field vs ['field'] vs GET_PATH(col, 'field') per dialect

These are applied after generation, deterministically, regardless of what the LLM emitted.

PART 3 — STATE OF THE ART

5. APEX-SQL — current academic/open SOTA

Paper: "APEX-SQL: Talking to the Data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" Authors: Bowen Cao, Weibin Liao, Yushi Sun et al. (CUHK / Peking University / Tencent Lightspeed) Venue: KDD 2026. arXiv: 2602.16720. Code: github.com/Tencent/APEX-SQL-Project

Core thesis: static schema representations fail to resolve semantic ambiguity in real enterprise databases (opaque column names, domain codes, value-format conventions). APEX-SQL shifts from "passive schema perception" to agentic exploration — it forms hypotheses about the data, verifies them by running SQL against the live database, and only then generates the answer.

Stage 1 — Schema Linking (4 steps)

Step 1: Hypothesis Generation (Logical Planning)

  • Generates N=2 schema-agnostic reasoning plans (temperature 0.8): solution steps in natural language ("filter by X, aggregate Y over Z") with no column names at all.
  • Aggregates to a single master plan (temperature 0.2).
  • Purpose: decouple intent parsing from schema vocabulary. The model doesn't latch onto superficially similar column names when it reasons without them.
  • Removing this step: −5 pp SRR on Spider 2.0-Snow (120-case pilot).

Example — schema-agnostic logical plan:

Question: "Considering only the latest release versions of NPM packages, which packages are the top 8 most popular based on GitHub stars, as well as their versions?"

1. Identify all packages in the NPM ecosystem.
2. For each package, identify release versions.
3. Determine which version is the latest release.
4. Link each package to its project or repository.
5. Get GitHub star count for each linked project.
6. Rank packages by star count descending.
7. Return package name and version for top 8.

Notice: no table names, no column names, no SQL — pure intent. Schema pruning and SQL generation happen in subsequent steps, guided by this plan.

Step 2: Dual-Pathway Pruning

  • Two simultaneous LLM passes over the full column set:
    • Negative pass: identify columns to delete (confidently irrelevant)
    • Positive pass: identify columns to keep (confidently needed)
  • Union logic: a column survives unless both passes reject it — high precision without sacrificing recall. Equivalent to a conservative AND of two independent pruning signals.
  • Compresses ~3 430 columns → ~383 columns (9× reduction, ~7k tokens).
  • Ablation (120-case pilot, Strict Recall Rate):
Pruning configuration SRR
Both passes (full) 97.5%
Selection pass only 93.3% (−4.2 pp)
Deletion pass only 80.8% (−16.7 pp)

Baseline ReFoRCE schema linking on the same protocol: 35.0% SRR.

Step 3: Parallel Data Profiling

  • Independent agents per table run role-specific exploratory SQL queries against the live database.
  • Validates each column's actual role: is it a real filter key, a join key, a metric, nullable? Not inferred from schema text — validated against actual value distributions.
  • Results >30 rows are compressed to top-10 + aggregate statistics.
  • Runs in parallel across tables for speed.
  • Removing this step: −9.2 pp SRR.

Step 4: Global Synthesis

  • Integrates all cross-table empirical observations.
  • Enforces topological connectivity: the output schema subgraph D* must have all join paths traversable. No dangling tables.
  • Includes a Semantic Linking sub-step that hypothesises table/column roles before profiling, directing the probes toward the most relevant areas.

Ablation on all Stage 1 verification sub-steps (120-case pilot):

Configuration SRR
With logical planning → full verification 77.5%
Without logical planning 72.5% (−5.0 pp)
Without Semantic Linking 63.3% (−14.2 pp)
Without Data Profiling 68.3% (−9.2 pp)
Without Global Synthesis 73.3% (−4.2 pp)
Without all agentic verification 55.8% (−21.7 pp)

Stage 2 — SQL Generation (pre-processing + agentic loop + selection)

Pre-processing A: Macro Plan Aggregation

Multiple reasoning paths from Stage 1 are consolidated into a single unified master plan injected into the agent's initial context. Prevents the agent from starting blind or from anchoring on a single reasoning path.

Example — consolidated macro plan (same NPM question):

1. Filter NPM packages.
2. Keep only release versions.
3. Identify latest release per package.
4. Join package versions to projects.
5. Rank by GitHub stars.
6. Return top 8 package names and versions.

Compared to the logical plan above, the macro plan is shorter and action-oriented — it drops the exploratory reasoning and keeps only the executable steps that guide SQL synthesis.

Pre-processing B: Deterministic Guidance Retrieval

A rule engine (not embedding retrieval) maps operational keywords extracted from the master plan to categories in a pre-built directive library ℳ containing 14 categories:

14-category directive library ℳ  (click to expand)
Category Triggered by keywords Directive injected into prompt
Evidence Enforcement always active "Reference only the tables and columns identified in the master plan. Do not introduce tables or columns absent from the retrieved schema evidence."
String Matching match, name, like, contains, search "Use ILIKE with LOWER() for case-insensitive string filters. Apply TRIM() before comparison when matching user-supplied strings. Use = only when the schema confirms exact-match semantics."
Output Columns return, show, output, display, list "SELECT only the columns explicitly requested. Alias each output column with the exact terminology used in the question. Do not add unrequested columns."
Table Selection table, from, source, dataset "Drive joins from the primary fact table in the plan. Use dimension/lookup tables only to resolve foreign keys or decode filter values — do not pull metric columns from them."
Column Interpretation null, missing, unit, value, flag, status "Treat NULL as 'no data' unless the schema documents a sentinel (e.g., -1 = unknown). Verify units before arithmetic — revenue may be stored in cents, distances in metres."
Schema Grounding always active "Use only the exact column and table names from the pruned schema. Do not infer or guess column names not present in the retrieved evidence."
Join Strategy join, relate, link, combine, merge "Use INNER JOIN only when every left-table row is guaranteed a match. Use LEFT JOIN when zero-match rows must be preserved. Verify join keys match on data type and encoding before joining."
Filter Implementation where, filter, exclude, only, except "Prefer independent subqueries (computed once) over correlated subqueries (computed per outer row). For NOT IN with nullable columns, use NOT EXISTS to avoid silent empty results."
Aggregation count, sum, average, total, group, per "Include every non-aggregated SELECT column in GROUP BY. Use COUNT(DISTINCT col) rather than COUNT(*) when deduplication is needed. Prefer window functions over self-joins for running totals and rankings."
Sorting and Limiting top, rank, order, first, last, limit "Always append NULLS LAST to ORDER BY unless NULLs-first is explicitly required. When using LIMIT, ensure ORDER BY is fully deterministic — add a tiebreaker column if the primary sort key has ties."
Multi-Step Logic then, after, step, compute, intermediate "Decompose queries with more than two logical steps into named CTEs. Name each CTE after its semantic role (e.g., filtered_orders, monthly_totals). Avoid deeply nested subqueries — flatten with CTEs instead."
SQL Syntax date, timestamp, epoch, cast, convert "Use TO_TIMESTAMP(col/1e6)::DATE for epoch-microsecond columns. Double-quote all identifiers. Use QUALIFY for window-function row filtering instead of a wrapping subquery."
Common Pitfalls between, range, boundary, missing, zero "For date ranges use >= start AND < end+1 day rather than BETWEEN unless both endpoints are explicitly inclusive. Verify that intermediate filters cannot silently produce an empty set that zeros the final result."
Advanced Patterns nested, array, variant, recursive, pivot, flatten "For VARIANT/ARRAY columns use LATERAL FLATTEN(input => col) and reference elements as f.value. For recursive graph traversal use WITH RECURSIVE with an explicit termination condition and a depth-limit guard."

The keyword-to-category mapping achieves >95% recall and is noise-free vs. fuzzy retrieval.

Ablation — adding deterministic guidance (EX@8 metric):

Model With guidance Without guidance Δ
GPT-4o 29.79% 26.04% +3.75%
GPT-5 47.92% 43.65% +4.27%
DeepSeek-R1 48.75% 47.50% +1.25%

Adding guidance also reduces the number of agentic rounds (R̄) without reducing meaningful query count — the agent is more directed.

Agentic Exploration Loop (max 40 actions, 56k token budget)

The agent begins each run with the verified schema D*, the master plan from pre-processing A, and the selected directives from ℳ. It then cycles through four action types until a candidate SQL passes CONFIRMATION or the budget is exhausted. SQL synthesis is force-triggered at 52k tokens to guarantee a candidate even if exploration is incomplete.

Action details:

PROFILING
Generates targeted read-only SQL probes against columns that appear in the current plan but still lack grounding evidence. Prioritises value distributions, NULL rates, FK integrity, and value ranges. Query results exceeding 30 rows are compressed to the top-10 rows plus summary statistics, keeping the context compact. Each round of PROFILING narrows the gap between the plan and the actual data — the agent sees real values before it writes SQL.
CONSOLIDATION
Triggered periodically when the interaction history grows large. Discards intermediate reasoning text while retaining all probe SQLs, their execution results, and the latest version of the consolidated plan. The compressed state uses far fewer tokens, effectively extending the useful action budget within the hard 56k limit. Without CONSOLIDATION, context bloat would exhaust the budget before enough evidence is gathered.
SQL SYNTHESIS
Maps all accumulated evidence (probe results, plan, directives, schema D*) to a physical Snowflake SQL query. Executed immediately after generation. On execution error the agent classifies the error type, appends it to context, and re-enters the loop for targeted repair (returning to PROFILING for additional evidence if needed). Also force-triggered at 52k tokens regardless of loop state, guaranteeing a candidate SQL before the 56k budget is exhausted.
CONFIRMATION
A secondary semantic alignment check before the candidate is accepted. Verifies three conditions: (1) the result shape is plausible — correct approximate row count, expected columns, no unexpectedly NULL critical fields; (2) the SQL logic matches the question intent; (3) the query aligns with the master plan. If all three pass, the candidate is emitted. A semantic mismatch appends a critique to context and re-enters the loop, directing the next SYNTHESIS attempt to address the identified gap.

8 independent runs → majority vote: the entire loop (PROFILING → CONSOLIDATION → SQL SYNTHESIS → CONFIRMATION) runs 8 times with independent seeds. Each run produces one candidate SQL. The 8 executed results are compared by majority vote; a reward model breaks ties.

Example: PROFILING session — sf_bq031 (NOAA weather, Rochester 8-day moving average)

Question asks for daily Rochester weather (Jan–Mar 2019) with 8-day moving averages and lag1–lag8 differences across temperature, precipitation, and wind speed. Before writing SQL, the agent probes three gaps: how is Rochester identified in the station table, what ELEMENT codes exist, and what is the date column format.

Probe 1 — resolve station identifier for "Rochester"
SELECT "STATION_ID", "NAME"
FROM NOAA_DATA.PUBLIC.GHCND_STATIONS
WHERE "NAME" ILIKE '%rochester%'
LIMIT 10
→ result (2 rows)
STATION_ID       | NAME
USW00014733      | ROCHESTER INTL AP, NY US
USC00307799      | ROCHESTER 2 SSE, NY US
Evidence: station_id = 'USW00014733' for the primary Rochester airport station.
Probe 2 — discover available ELEMENT codes and their coverage
SELECT "ELEMENT", COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM NOAA_DATA.PUBLIC.GHCND_OBSERVATIONS
WHERE "STATION_ID" = 'USW00014733'
  AND "DATE" BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC
LIMIT 15
→ result (6 rows)
ELEMENT  | CNT
TMAX     |  90
TMIN     |  90
PRCP     |  88
SNOW     |  62
AWND     |  87
SNWD     |  61
Evidence: TMAX/TMIN = temperature (tenths of °C → divide by 10), PRCP = precipitation, AWND = average wind speed. All three target variables present for ≥87/90 days.
Probe 3 — verify DATE column format and value range
SELECT MIN("DATE"), MAX("DATE"), COUNT(DISTINCT "DATE")
FROM NOAA_DATA.PUBLIC.GHCND_OBSERVATIONS
WHERE "STATION_ID" = 'USW00014733'
→ result (1 row)
MIN("DATE")  | MAX("DATE")  | COUNT(DISTINCT "DATE")
1893-01-01   | 2024-11-30   | 47892
Evidence: DATE is a native DATE type — compare using DATE literals, not YYYYMMDD integers. Full historical record available.
Accumulated evidence passed to SQL SYNTHESIS:
Station = USW00014733 · Elements: TMAX (÷10 → °C), PRCP (÷10 → mm → cm), AWND (÷10 → m/s) · DATE is native DATE type · All three elements present ≥97% of days in target range
Example: SQL SYNTHESIS → error → CONFIRMATION — sf_bq050 (Citibike + weather + geo join)

Question requires joining bike trips with Central Park weather data and ZIP-code polygon boundaries to aggregate trip stats by neighborhood pair. Three-source join with a geospatial point-in-polygon predicate and an integer YYYYMMDD date column in the weather table.

SQL SYNTHESIS — attempt 1 (date format error)
SELECT z."NEIGHBORHOOD" AS start_neighborhood, z2."NEIGHBORHOOD" AS end_neighborhood,
       COUNT(*) AS total_trips, ...
FROM NEW_YORK_CITIBIKE_1.CYCLISTIC.BIKESHARE_TRIPS t
JOIN NEW_YORK_CITIBIKE_1.CYCLISTIC.CENTRAL_PARK_WEATHER w
  ON TO_DATE(TO_VARCHAR(w."DATE"), 'YYYYMMDD') = DATE_TRUNC('day', t."STARTTIME")
JOIN GEO_US_BOUNDARIES.PUBLIC.ZIP_CODES z
  ON ST_WITHIN(ST_POINT(t."START_STATION_LONGITUDE", t."START_STATION_LATITUDE"),
               z."ZIP_CODE_GEOM")
...
Execution error: SQL compilation error: invalid identifier 'ZIP_CODE_GEOM' — column not found in table GEO_US_BOUNDARIES.PUBLIC.ZIP_CODES
Loop action: classify as OBJECT_NOT_FOUND → probe correct geometry column name → re-enter PROFILING
PROFILING — targeted repair probe
SELECT column_name, data_type
FROM GEO_US_BOUNDARIES.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS
WHERE table_name = 'ZIP_CODES'
ORDER BY ordinal_position
→ result (5 rows)
COLUMN_NAME          | DATA_TYPE
ZIP_CODE             | TEXT
STATE_CODE           | TEXT
BOROUGH              | TEXT
NEIGHBORHOOD         | TEXT
GEO                  | GEOGRAPHY
Evidence: geometry column is "GEO" (GEOGRAPHY type), not "ZIP_CODE_GEOM". ST_WITHIN needs ST_GEOGPOINT() not ST_POINT() for Snowflake GEOGRAPHY.
SQL SYNTHESIS — attempt 2 (date format also fixed from earlier probe)
JOIN NEW_YORK_CITIBIKE_1.CYCLISTIC.CENTRAL_PARK_WEATHER w
  ON w."DATE" = CAST(TO_CHAR(t."STARTTIME"::DATE, 'YYYYMMDD') AS INTEGER)
JOIN GEO_US_BOUNDARIES.PUBLIC.ZIP_CODES z
  ON ST_WITHIN(ST_GEOGPOINT(t."START_STATION_LONGITUDE", t."START_STATION_LATITUDE"),
               z."GEO")
Execution success: 847 rows returned · ~2.3s
CONFIRMATION check
Result shape plausible? 847 neighborhood pairs for a full year — reasonable for NYC borough granularity. ✓
SQL logic matches intent? Groups by start/end neighborhood, aggregates trip count, avg duration, avg weather metrics, derives peak month. ✓
Aligns with master plan? All six requested output columns present; weather join on trip date matches plan. ✓
PASS → candidate SQL accepted (run 1 of 8)

6. Other SOTA methods

DivSkill-SQL (Spider 2.0-Lite SOTA, 73.1%)

What it is: current top performer on Spider 2.0-Lite. Addresses the core weakness of naive ensembling — when all candidates fail the same way, generating more of them does not help.

Key idea — Residual Skill Optimization: instead of random prompt diversity, it builds a growing library of complementary "skills" (prompt + strategy recipes). Each new skill is trained specifically on the examples the current ensemble still gets wrong, explicitly maximising Pass@K — the probability that at least one of K candidates is correct. This means each new skill patches the blind spots of the previous ones rather than duplicating their strengths.

At inference time, multiple skill-guided agents each solve the query via structurally different interaction patterns; final selection chooses across them.

Measured effect: 3× fewer hallucinated schema/function references vs. stochastic ensembling, because skill-targeted agents learn to avoid specific schema-linking failure modes.
Why it outperforms random Best-of-N: failure-targeted diversity — each skill covers exactly the gap the others leave. Random temperature sampling cannot guarantee this.

DSR-SQL (Dual-State Reasoning, mid-tier)

What it is: a two-phase architecture that separates schema compression from SQL synthesis, running them as distinct reasoning states rather than collapsing both into one generation prompt.

State 1 — Adaptive context (schema compression): an LLM writes exploratory SQL and samples the schema 3× at high temperature, then merges the results — retaining only the tables and columns that appear relevant across samples. This compresses a 3 000+ column warehouse down to a focused slice before generation begins.

State 2 — Progressive generation (4-state machine): SQL is built incrementally, one sub-question at a time, with each intermediate result executed before the next step is taken:

  • Extend: generate the next sub-question step
  • Revise: fix the last step if execution returned an error or wrong result
  • Explore: probe real data when the result looks suspicious
  • Rephrase: finalise the complete assembled query

Also includes evidence extraction: external documents (table descriptions, data dictionaries) are compressed down to the specific facts and formulas the current question needs, rather than injecting the full document into the prompt.

ReFoRCE (prior academic SOTA on Snow, 31% with o1-preview)

What it is: the previous academic state-of-the-art on Spider 2.0-Snow, achieving 31% with o1-preview. Combines schema compression, pre-generation data exploration, output format enforcement, and voting-based selection.

Four mechanisms:

  1. Table compression: groups near-duplicate and date-sharded tables; prunes columns so 3 000+ column schemas fit within context limits without truncation.
  2. Column exploration: runs probe SQL before generating the answer — SELECT DISTINCT, value samples, nested-field inspection — feeding real values and data formats back as grounding context. This is the same motivation as our exploration front-end (§3c).
  3. Format restriction: derives the expected answer's column structure and output types from the question, then forces the generated SQL to match — reducing wrong-shape and wrong-column answers.
  4. Self-refinement + self-consistency voting: generates multiple candidates, repairs each on execution feedback independently, then selects by majority vote — the answer that multiple independent repair paths agree on wins.

Schema linking comparison: ReFoRCE achieves 35% Schema Retrieval Rate vs. APEX-SQL's 97.5% on Spider 2.0-Snow — a 62 pp gap explained by APEX-SQL's hypothesis-driven dual-pathway pruning and data-profiling verification steps that ReFoRCE lacks.

7. Databricks Genie — commercial architecture

Product: AI/BI Genie — conversational NL-to-SQL, part of the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform. GA: June 2025. No public Spider 2.0 / BIRD benchmark numbers published.

Fundamental design philosophy: the opposite of APEX-SQL. Instead of runtime schema exploration, Genie invests up-front expert curation to narrow the LLM's task. Domain experts build a Genie Space; at query time the LLM selects from pre-verified patterns rather than reasoning over the full schema from scratch.

The Genie Space — configuration unit

Resource Hard limit Contents
Tables / views 30 Unity Catalog tables scoped to this domain
Knowledge store snippets 200 Column descriptions, SQL expressions (KPIs, filters, row transforms), join definitions, synonyms
Instructions 100 Parameterized example SQL + general text rules (effective up to ~20 lines)
Entity matching 120 columns, 1 024 values each Pre-sampled distinct-value lists for categoricals

5-layer schema linking

  1. Unity Catalog metadata (always active): schema, types, PK/FK, column descriptions.
  2. Intelligent filtering (mechanism not disclosed — likely BM25/embedding): selects relevant columns and example SQL from the Space at query time.
  3. Entity matching: pre-sampled distinct-value lists. Resolves "Florida" → WHERE state = 'FL'; "first level support" → exact DB code. Filters appear as dropdowns in the UI.
  4. Join relationships: explicit definitions in the knowledge store; auto-suggested from FK metadata.
  5. Genie Ontology (workspace-wide, announced June 2026): automatic semantic map built from tables, dashboards, notebooks, and 50+ connected apps including Google Drive, SharePoint, Slack, and Jira.

LLM backbone — compound AI with model rotation

Mode Primary model
Standard Genie Spaces Azure OpenAI (primary)
Agent Mode / Research Agent Anthropic Claude Sonnet (explicitly documented)
Partner AI disabled Databricks-hosted open-weight fallback

Databricks rotates models without disclosure; two upgrades documented (Nov 2024, Sep 2025).

Agentic evolution

Date Capability added
Early 2025 Chain-of-Thought reasoning — thinking steps shown per response
2025 Self-reflection — checks own SQL before execution
Late 2025 Research Agent (beta) — single unified reasoning agent; uses Claude Sonnet
Dec 2025 Semantic ambiguity detection — asks clarifying questions
Apr 2026 Agent Mode public preview (UI only; not exposed via API)

Trusted Assets — the key structural differentiator

  • Parameterized example SQL: if user question matches a trusted asset's NL question, Genie runs the verified SQL directly (parameter-substituted), bypassing LLM generation entirely. Response is flagged "Trusted."
  • SQL UDFs (Unity Catalog): exact function logic executes, always "Trusted."
  • For high-frequency or high-stakes queries, the LLM is completely eliminated from the path.

Key tradeoff

Genie trades setup cost (expert curation of knowledge stores, entity lists, trusted assets) for runtime reliability and governance. APEX-SQL and ReFoRCE do zero setup and explore at runtime; Genie offloads that cost to up-front domain investment.

10. Where we stand and what closing the gap requires

The gap to APEX-SQL is architectural, not tuning.

APEX-SQL's advantage on Spider 2.0-Snow comes from data-grounded exploration during schema linking — its 97.5% SRR vs our retrieval-based approach on the same schemas. Our Best-of-N + deterministic compiler is effective on conventional schemas but doesn't resolve the fundamental "which column actually means what" ambiguity in enterprise DBs.

Specific gaps and what fills them:

Gap What APEX-SQL does Our path
Schema ambiguity resolution Parallel data profiling — runs SQL to validate column roles Wire exploration front-end into schema-linking stage (currently post-linking)
Large column space Dual-pathway pruning (9× compression, 97.5% SRR) SchemaSlice is partial; add hypothesis-driven filtering
SQL format correctness 14-category deterministic tip library Plan→SQL compiler already addresses this; extend to geo
Answer selection Reward model + 8 candidates Learned verifier (training code exists; not trained yet)
Geospatial queries Not specialised for geo PlanGeoJoin/PlanGeoFilter compiler extension

Common Winning Ingredients — Across All Leading Systems

# Ingredient Evidence
1 Strong base model Gates everything — gpt-5.4-mini yields no gain from the architecture; gpt-5.4 yields +400%
2 Ground in real data before generating APEX Stage 1 profiling, ReFoRCE column exploration, our exploration front-end — all probe actual values/formats before writing SQL
3 Many diverse candidates + smart selection Removing Best-of-N costs −80 pp in our ablation; APEX Pass@8 gap is −15 pp; DivSkill-SQL is built entirely around this
4 Iterative verify-and-refine with execution feedback Every leading system runs the SQL, inspects the result, and repairs — not a single-shot generation
5 Schema linking / pruning / compression Enterprise warehouses have 3 000+ columns — retrieval quality directly bounds accuracy ceiling (SRR: ReFoRCE 35% vs. APEX-SQL 97.5%)
6 Dialect discipline — deterministic, not soft prompting Model priors override prompt hints for date encoding, LATERAL FLATTEN, recursive CTEs; correct patterns must be enforced in code

Our ablation confirms #3 is dominant. Our contribution is #2 (value/format grounding) and #6 (deterministic compiler). The leaders' edge is primarily #4 (full hypothesis-verify loops) and heavier #3.
